In terms of weight loss:

In semaglutide, it’s largely just changing appetite and satiety. A big calories in adjustment. 

In tirzepatide, it also changes appetite and cravings, and also fat oxidation but not to the extent that it changes energy expenditure (calories out). When you lose weight, your energy expenditure (EE) usually drops as your weight decreases, which is called metabolic adaptation. In a mouse study with tirzepatide, they found it attenuated metabolic adaptation meaning that it reduced the amount that the energy expenditure dropped, but in tests on humans, the energy expenditure drop remained proportional to what those who lost weight on placebo experienced - so no change to metabolic adaptation.

I believe Novo has run experiments on CagriSema showing a more pronounced reduction in metabolic adaptation in rats, but it remains to be seen if that will translate to humans.

Lilly has also run human a human trial much like the tirzepatide EE trial for the upcoming retatrutide, but they have not released those results yet.  Because Reta adds glucagon, it’s anticipated there will be an EE change in those results, but results are TBD. Hopefully Lilly will release that info this summer.

They all certainly do adjust other metabolic processes - that’s why they are used to treat a type 2 diabetes, providing better blood sugar control, but that does not appear to meaningfully adjust EE. They also have plenty of other benefits in the kidneys, liver, heart, etc, but that’s outside the weight loss discussion.

With semaglutide going off-patent in the Indian market, we are about to see a massive surge in its usage for both diabetes and obesity. As an ophthalmologist, I believe it is important to look beyond the metabolic benefits and address the fine print that often gets lost in the excitement.

One of the most common complaints we'll likely hear is blurred vision. It is important to educate patients that this is often a refractive shift rather than permanent damage; rapid fluctuations in blood sugar can cause the lens of the eye to swell or shrink, leading to temporary blurring.

We also need to be proactive about drug-induced dry eye disease. Emerging evidence suggests GLP-1 RAs may induce dry eye by altering the production or composition of the tear film. This can lead to a gritty sensation and further blurred vision, which we can help manage with lifestyle modifications or ocular lubricants.

However, the more serious concerns; Nonarteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (NAION) and the early worsening of Diabetic Retinopathy (DR), require attention. While data is mixed, some large cohort studies have shown a threefold higher risk of NAION in semaglutide users. Furthermore, the rapid drop in HbA1c can paradoxically trigger DR progression, likely due to osmotic shifts, altered VEGF signalling, and the breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier.

The real clinical challenge we face is the lack of clear guidelines. While the ADA standards of care advise assessing a patient’s DR status before starting or escalating GLP-1 RA treatment, they do not specify how often follow-up eye exams should be performed in this specific context.

Given the impending explosion of these prescriptions in India, here is my approach:
Baseline retinal evaluation: We must know the state of the retina before the rapid glycemic shift begins.
High risk eyes: Patients with pre-existing severe NPDR or proliferative DR need much tighter monitoring.
Patient education: We must teach patients to distinguish between temporary refractive blur and the sudden, painless vision loss associated with NAION.

Don’t make a meal of your business lunch. Here are 20 rules that’ll help you avoid a two-course ordeal

A business lunch can be a fine thing. Over a couple of courses, you can find common ground, show your appreciation and navigate what might have seemed like a tricky relationship when it was all taking place online. But after years of video calls and working from home, people have grown shy of the idea. So here’s a starter pack of advice.
1.
You will probably have between an hour and 90 minutes so ensure that you choose the restaurant wisely. Tasting menus and wine pairings are painful at the best of times. At lunch, they are like a kidnapping with compote. Oh, and no sharing concepts.

2.
The restaurant should be easy to find. Your counterparts shouldn’t need the skills of Sir Ranulph Fiennes to locate “this really cool place that I’ve heard about”. You want this friendship – meet in the middle and respect their time.

3.
Don’t be scared to go low. It won’t work every time but sometimes modesty is the best policy. Fish and chips? Why not?

4.
No laptops or phones. It’s a restaurant, not the Apple Store.

5.
An emergency call from the office? You may go outside once. But you are already losing the room. Twice? It will look as though you’re having an affair or are just rude.
📷

6.
Know your neighbours. Don’t wander into sensitive territory and ask financial questions if half of the people in the club or restaurant are in the same trade as you. And if the key numbers can’t be written down on the back of a napkin, don’t attempt to pick apart spreadsheet-level details while dissecting a guinea fowl.

7.
Arrive on time. Sorry, I don’t care if your husband lost a leg this morning. The clock is ticking.

8.
Here are the lateness rules. Ten minutes are forgivable (ask the maître d’ for a newspaper or have an emergency novel in your pocket; don’t just scroll). Twenty minutes late? They’re paying. Thirty minutes? Have a nice lunch and finish your book.

9.
Be interesting. The best business lunches are with people who know stuff and can tell a story or two. No, they don’t want to see pictures of your children.

10.
Shut up. Listen. It’s a rare skill but one you should perfect.

11.
If you are American, don’t look horrified when a European orders a glass of wine at lunch. No intervention is needed.

12.
If you’re jabbing your thigh with semaglutide these days and have the appetite of a dormouse, why did you come? As soon as you asked the waiter if they could do a half-portion of the rocket salad, this was over.

13.
“I won’t have bread but if you want it, please go ahead.” Really, avoid all virtue signalling when ordering. Show that you’re the kind of person who knows how to let everyone get what they want from an agreement – even when it’s just the breadbasket that’s at stake. 

14.
Be decent. That means to the restaurant staff too. At the end of a very nice lunch this week, my guest said to the waiter, “Your service has been exceptional. Indeed, it was a highlight of the meal.” It was one of those small interactions that underlined why I love working with this writer.

15.
How many courses? Having just a starter and a main is the industry standard. Just a main is also fine, though it can imply that you would rather be out of there. Puddings? They can work but the lunch now risks resembling a family outing with grandma.

16.
Coffee? Ordering espressos with the bill will leave everyone feeling caffeinated and on schedule. “Can I have a pot of your green tea?” is a sentence that will cause anxiety levels to rise among your fellow diners.

17.
Who’s paying? Splitting a bill for a business lunch is rarely wise. If you’re the one who selected the venue and set the dining pace, just pay. If your counterpart has been ascending to the Himalayan heights of the wine menu or ordering a labrador-sized steak, sit back.
 
18.
No doggy bags. You might not like to waste food but unless you’re working for an NGO, taking away a tub of slowly congealing dauphinoise potatoes won’t make you look cool, just parsimonious.

19.
They paid? Say thank you. 

20.
You paid? Say thank you for their time and for being good company. Well, only if they were.

A recent study from University of Cambridge researchers, published in eClinicalMedicine, raises serious red flags about what happens when people stop GLP-1 medications like Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, or Zepbound after major weight loss.
The analysis drew from six rigorous randomized trials involving over 3,200 participants. The results are alarming:
• Within just one year of stopping, people regain about 60% of the weight they lost.
• Over longer periods, regain can climb to as much as 75%, with most of it returning within roughly 60 weeks.
• Only about 25% of the initial loss seems to stay off long-term.
Even more disturbing is the impact on body composition: 40–60% of the weight lost on these drugs often comes from lean muscle mass, not just fat.
When the weight rebounds—and it usually does—it comes back primarily as fat.
This leaves many people in a worse spot than before: higher body fat percentage, reduced muscle, weakened metabolism, lower strength, and increased long-term health risks, including greater vulnerability to conditions like sarcopenia in older adults.
High discontinuation rates compound the problem—around half of users stop within the first year due to intolerable side effects, high costs, or access barriers—triggering this rapid, often devastating rebound.
These drugs can deliver impressive short-term results for obesity and type 2 diabetes, affecting over a billion people worldwide.
But the evidence shows they're far from a simple or safe fix.
Without aggressive countermeasures—like resistance training, high protein intake, and sustained lifestyle changes—muscle loss accelerates, and stopping the drug frequently undoes progress while leaving lasting damage.
If you're on these medications or considering them, insist on a detailed discussion with your doctor: body composition monitoring, strength-focused exercise plans, and a realistic strategy for maintenance or safe discontinuation.
Beyond the rebound and muscle wasting, other reported concerning side effects include persistent gastrointestinal issues (severe nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation), gallbladder problems (gallstones, cholecystitis), pancreatitis (inflammation of the pancreas, which can be life-threatening and has led to reported deaths), potential risks of thyroid tumors or cancer (noted in animal studies and carrying FDA boxed warnings, though human evidence remains inconclusive), kidney issues, vision problems like non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), and more.
In light of the rapid regain, significant muscle loss, high dropout rates, and these additional serious risks, the risks are rarely worth the benefits for most people seeking sustainable weight management.

By William Wallace, PhD.

The "Quarter Rule" in body composition research holds that roughly 25% of weight lost during calorie restriction comes from lean mass rather than fat. This ratio has been consistent across meta-analyses of dietary interventions and holds for bariatric surgery in a similar range (~20-24% depending on procedure type).

DXA substudies from the major GLP-1 and GLP-1/GIP trials show most incretin therapies landing in the same neighborhood. Tirzepatide (SURMOUNT-1, 72 weeks) produced 21.3% total body weight loss with 26% of that loss attributable to lean mass.

Liraglutide came in at 16% in a smaller cohort (6 months). Both figures fall within the expected range for any equivalent calorie deficit.

Semaglutide is the notable exception. In the STEP 1 DXA substudy (68 weeks), 40% of total weight lost was lean mass. Other semaglutide datasets report lower figures (the COURAGE trial measured ~35%), suggesting 40% may represent the upper bound, but even the lower estimates exceed the diet-only benchmark.

An important measurement caveat: DXA quantifies "lean body mass," which includes water, organ tissue, and connective tissue in addition to skeletal muscle. A portion of measured lean loss reflects adaptive tissue remodeling during weight reduction, not direct muscle catabolism.

All trials included lifestyle counseling, but none required resistance training or set specific protein targets. A recent case series of patients who combined incretin therapy with resistance training (3-5 sessions/week) and protein intakes ranging from 0.7-1.7 g/kg/day found that one patient lost 6.9% lean mass despite 33% total weight loss, and two patients with higher protein intakes actually gained lean mass while losing 13-27% of body weight.

The irony of this conversation is that the people most alarmed about GLP-1 muscle loss are fitness-conscious people who already lift and eat adequate protein. They are the least likely to have a "problem". The people at actual risk are sedentary patients with low baseline protein intake and no training history. They are probably not reading this post.

GLP-1s produce substantially more total weight loss than calorie restriction alone, which means more absolute lean mass is lost. But for most of these drugs, the proportional ratio is not meaningfully different from dieting. The clinical variable that appears to matter most is not which drug is prescribed but whether the prescribing protocol includes resistance training and adequate protein intake alongside it.

Yes, energy balance matters. No one disputes that. But the body is not a passive furnace where calories go in and heat comes out. It’s a hormonal system that actively regulates hunger, energy expenditure, and fat storage.

We’ve known for decades that genetics influence body weight. Twin and adoption studies consistently show 40–70% heritability of BMI. And specific variants such as those in the FTO gene affect appetite regulation and energy balance.

More importantly, when people lose weight the body fights back. Hormones change:
•Leptin drops
•Ghrelin rises
•Resting metabolic rate decreases

This phenomenon—called adaptive thermogenesis—is why long-term weight maintenance is difficult even for highly disciplined people.

That’s also why modern treatments like Semaglutide and Tirzepatide work. They change the hormonal signals that regulate hunger and metabolism. If obesity were simply a “discipline problem,” these medications wouldn’t produce the large, reproducible weight loss seen in randomized trials.

So the short version:

Calories matter.
But biology decides how hungry you are, how efficiently you burn those calories, and how hard your body fights weight loss.

Calling that “just discipline” is not physiology. It’s moralizing.

Blockbuster Weight Loss Drugs Under the Microscope

GLP-1 medications like semaglutide and tirzepatide have transformed obesity treatment — helping people lose substantial weight, improve blood sugar control, and even lower cardiovascular risk. For many, they’ve been life-changing.

But a recent report in Nature highlights fresh scrutiny: regulators in the UK and Brazil are reviewing reports of pancreatitis (inflammation of the pancreas) in some patients using these drugs.

Here’s what research shows so far.

In the large clinical trials that led to approval, pancreatitis cases were recorded — but they were rare. Some pooled analyses of multiple trials suggest there could be a small increase in risk compared to placebo. However, other large studies, including real-world database analyses, have not found a statistically significant rise in pancreatitis among users.

One major challenge: the very people prescribed these drugs often already have risk factors for pancreatitis — obesity, gallstones, high triglycerides, and type 2 diabetes. That makes it difficult to determine whether the drug is the cause or whether the underlying metabolic condition plays a major role.

What is clearly established is that these drugs affect the gut. They mimic the GLP-1 hormone, which slows stomach emptying and reduces appetite. That’s why nausea, vomiting, and constipation are common early side effects. Rare but serious gastrointestinal complications have been reported, but considering the millions of prescriptions worldwide, severe events remain uncommon.

This situation reflects how modern medicine works. When a drug becomes widely used, rare adverse events may begin to surface. Regulators investigate. Researchers analyze larger datasets. Risk is quantified more precisely over time.

Obesity itself is not a cosmetic issue — it significantly raises the risk of diabetes, heart disease, stroke, and early mortality. Any therapy must be judged against that backdrop.

The key question isn’t whether a medication has any risk — almost all effective drugs do. The real question is whether the benefits outweigh the risks for a particular individual. And based on current evidence, while vigilance is warranted, these medications remain powerful and generally safe tools in the fight against obesity.

Key evidence from randomized trials (e.g., 52-week semaglutide vs placebo in high-fracture-risk adults; JAMA Network Open on GLP-1 + exercise):
- Bone resorption rises and BMD drops at weight-bearing sites (spine/hip) with greater weight loss on the drug.
- No changes at non-weight-bearing sites (e.g., distal radius), pointing to loading, not direct pharmacology.
- When exercise is added (matching or exceeding weight loss), BMD is preserved despite more loss.
- Studies equating or controlling for weight changes (or in diabetics with less net loss) show no extra bone impact from the GLP-1.

The patients using compounded semaglutide through platforms like Hims were largely cash-pay consumers locked out of branded Wegovy by Medicare's statutory prohibition on covering weight loss drugs and PBM prior authorization walls. That said, your instinct that this ends badly is correct, just for structural reasons more than DOJ ones. Hims built a material revenue stream on a legal justification that had an expiration date baked into it: FDA drug shortage listings. Once Novo Nordisk resolved manufacturing constraints and announced shortage resolution in late 2024, the entire regulatory basis for mass-distributed compounded semaglutide collapsed. FDA enforcement was not a surprise. It was the predictable endpoint of a model that depended on a temporary condition the original manufacturer had every incentive to fix.

The deeper story is what this reveals about how venture capital prices regulatory risk in healthcare. The billion-dollar compounded GLP-1 market got capitalized as if enforcement timelines were indefinitely deferrable. They were not. And the FDA warning letter landing right as Hims committed to a Super Bowl ad slot for weight loss offerings was not coincidence, it was a coordinated brand protection move alongside Novo Nordisk's simultaneous lawsuit.

[4/1/2026] FDA reminds compounders certain conditions must be met for compounded drugs to qualify for the exemptions under sections 503A and 503B of the FD&C Act, including the highlights below.

Under section 503A:

The drug product is compounded for an individual patient based on receipt of a prescription. 

The compounder does not compound, regularly or in inordinate amounts, any that are essentially copies of a commercially available drug product.

As stated in guidance, the agency intends to consider a compounded drug product to be essentially a copy of a commercially available drug product if:

•the compounded drug product has the same active pharmaceutical ingredient(s) (API) as the commercially available drug product in the same, similar or an easily substitutable strength, and

•the commercially available drug product can be used by the same route of administration (regardless of how it is labeled) prescribed for the compounded drug product.

This is unless a prescriber determines and documents the compounded drug product contains a change that produces a significant difference from the commercially available drug product for an identified individual patient.  

FDA intends to consider a compounded drug product to be essentially a copy of a commercially available drug product if: 

•the compounded drug product contains the same APIs as two or more commercially available drug products in the same, similar or easily substitutable strength and
•the commercially available drug product can be used (regardless of how it is labeled) by the same route of administration prescribed for the compounded drug product, unless there is documentation of a prescriber determination of a significant difference.

For example, FDA may consider a compounded drug product that combines semaglutide API and another API, such as vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin), to be essentially a copy of a commercially available drug product when the:

•drug products are used by the same route of administration – the compounded drug product is given the same way as the commercially available drug products, such as an injectable 
•drug products are the same, similar or easily substitutable strength – the amounts of semaglutide and vitamin B12 in the compounded drug product are within 10% of the strengths of the respective commercially available drug products.

FDA has stated, at this time, it does not intend to take action against a compounder for compounding a drug product that is essentially a copy of a commercially available drug product regularly or in inordinate amounts if the compounder fills four or fewer prescriptions of that compounded drug product during a calendar month.

The GLP-1 world right now has three separate fights happening at once

Fight 1 - Semaglutide just went generic in India

Semaglutide patent expired March 20. Over 50 companies are jumping in. Natco is selling it at ₹1,290/month, that's a 90% price drop from ₹15,000+. 

For a country with 135 million diabetics and 250 million overweight people, this is like opening a dam. 

Millions who could never afford these drugs suddenly can. That's the public health earthquake.

But this is a commodity war. When 50 companies sell the same molecule, nobody makes fat margins. It becomes a volume game with razor-thin profits. 

Fight 2 - Tirzepatide vs Semaglutide - the drug war

At top dose, tirzepatide gives 15% weight loss. Semaglutide gives 10%. That's not a small gap  tirzepatide is 50% better. 

semaglutide is going generic in 10+ countries this year, so Novo loses pricing power. Tirzepatide stays patent-protected. 

Lilly wins on both fronts - better drug AND full pricing power. Novo is already cutting prices to fight generics

Divi's picked a side here, they're making the building blocks for Lilly tirzepatide, not jumping into the semaglutide generic dogfight. 

Fight 3 - Injections vs Pills 

This is where it gets really interesting 

Right now, Divi is building massive peptide synthesis capacity (Kakinada plant, solid-phase peptide synthesis). This is perfect for injectable tirzepatide  complex peptide molecules that need specialized manufacturing.

But two oral pills are coming fast:

Novo oral Wegovy (25mg pill, approved Dec 2025) gives 16.6% weight loss - matching injections. 

But it's still a peptide, still needs empty stomach, 30-minute wait. Still complex to manufacture. So Divi peptide capacity stays relevant here.

Lilly's orforglipron (FDA decision expected April 2026) is the wild card. It a small molecule, not a peptide. No food restrictions. No waiting. 

Starter dose at $149/month in the US - clearly a mass-market volume play. If this wins the convenience war (and for a daily pill taken by millions, convenience beats an extra 4% weight loss), then the entire manufacturing game changes. 

Small molecule manufacturing is totally different from peptide synthesis. Divi peptide capacity becomes less relevant for the oral volume war.

So where does Divi's actually sit?

The best case - injectable tirzepatide isn't going away anytime soon. Even if orforglipron wins the mass market, injectables will remain the premium option for patients who want maximum weight loss. 

Hospitals, specialists, severe obesity cases, they'll keep using injectables. And Lilly needs massive volumes of peptide intermediates for that. 

Divi is one of very few Indian companies that can deliver at scale and quality. Jefferies sees $800M-$1B in GLP-1 revenue for Divi by FY32.

Novo pricing Wegovy at $249-$329/month is a direct response to the compounding market they just helped kill. That's not a coincidence in timing. They spent months lobbying FDA, resolved their shortage, filed suit against Hims, and now they're launching a subscription program at price points that would have seemed unthinkable a year ago. The compounders forced Novo's hand on pricing even as they were being regulated out of existence.

This is actually the most interesting outcome of the whole saga. The patient access argument that compounders used to justify their model turned out to be correct, at least in terms of market impact. Compounded semaglutide at $200-300/month created a price ceiling that Novo now has to compete under. The gray market shaped the legitimate market even after enforcement ended it.

The question now is whether $249/month is sustainable for Novo long-term, or whether this is an introductory price designed to recapture the customer segment that was being served by compounders. Either way, patients who were worried about losing access to affordable GLP-1s after FDA enforcement got a version of what they needed, just from the brand manufacturer instead of a telehealth platform.

Are we on the cusp of a "peptide" revolution?

People keep saying “GLP-1s are peptides and they work, so peptides work.” But GLP-1s are actually a good example of the opposite:
 
Even when you have a biologically real target and a real signal, it can still take years of optimization, iteration, dosing work, formulation work, and large randomized trials before you get something that produces robust, effects.

The biology was identified in the 1980s, but native GLP-1 has a half-life of only about 1–2 minutes, so it was never going to become a major therapy in its natural form.

Liraglutide (Novo Nordisk) was first approved for diabetes in 2010, and only later for obesity in 2014. 

In other words, even with a real target and real biology, it took around 25 years to get from discovery to a meaningful obesity medicine.

And even then, liraglutide was not the modern GLP-1 story people now have in mind. At obesity dose, it produced about 8% average weight loss at 56 weeks versus about 2.6% for placebo. Important, yes. Transformative, not yet. 

The much bigger effects associated with this class came later, after further engineering by Novo and others, especially with molecules like semaglutide, which delivered longer exposure, more sustained receptor activity, and more practical dosing.

===========================
Native peptide biology is *not the same thing* as a useful therapeutic.
===========================

A peptide with an interesting mechanism can still fail in practice because:
- it is degraded too quickly
- it does not reach the right tissues in the right way
- the effect size is too small
- the dosing is impractical
- side effects limit adherence
- early studies are noisy, underpowered, or not reproducible

That is why GLP-1s don't somehow validate every peptide currently circulating in the longevity, fitness, or optimization world, whether BPC-157 or any other peptide of the month.

Some of these compounds may have real effects.

But those effects may also be small, inconsistent, context-dependent, or clinically irrelevant.

When the RCT base is thin, inconsistent, or missing, updating toward caution makes sense.

Anecdotes, mechanistic plausibility, and even early positive data are not enough.

The question is whether a therapeutic survives the filters that separate hype from medicine:
- randomized controls
- clear endpoints
- dose standardization
- adverse event tracking
- replication
- longitudinal follow-up
- real denominator data, not just testimonials

If a company wants to make peptides easy to buy, fine.
But we should also track outcomes with similar energy.

This includes:
- baseline data collection
- protocol tracking
- outcome measurement
- side effect reporting
- follow-up over time
- public learning from aggregate results

This does not have to happen only through the traditional pharma model. It can also happen through decentralized evidence platforms and structured real-world outcome tracking, including approaches - e.g. @radiclescience (no affiliation).

The standard should be simple:

On the one hand, it makes sense to allow people to try things and let the market help discovery.

At the same time, if you want to sell people on a molecule or biologic, you should also want to measure what it actually does.

And keep in mind that small molecules can already be sold under the GRAS pathway (10x faster and cheaper than full Phase 1-3 trials), including completely synthetic molecules not found in natures.

What we are missing is a proper pathway to evaluate health improving interventions, not merely disease-addressing interventions.

Such a pathway would create a faster and cheaper path to market, assuming safety is proven, and create a set of processes to collect data and establish effect and efficacy of such interventions.

Guidelines for managing diabetes, including recommendationsfor retinopathy assessment and monitoring, are provided by the current American Diabetes Association (ADA) standards of care. Since GLP‑1 RAs have been associated with retinal deterioration, the standards specifically advise assessing the patient’s diabetic retinopathy status before starting or escalating GLP‑1 RA treatment.  

However, the standards do not specify how often eye exams should be performed in this context. If a patient experiences vision loss while using semaglutide, the American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) recommends stopping the medication until an ophthalmologist has performed a comprehensive eye exam. 

Clinicians should adhere to the general guidelines for retinopathy screening and monitoring as outlined in standards of care, which vary depending on the severity of retinopathy.  

Typically, patients without diabetic retinopathy should be monitored every 1–2 years, those with mild nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR) should have annual follow‑ups, patients with moderate NPDR should be checked every 6–9 months and referred to an ophthalmologist within 3–6 months, and patients with severe NPDR should be reviewed every 3–6 months and referred immediately to an ophthalmologist. The ADA emphasizes the importance of managing diabetes from a patient‑centered approach.  

While the standards of care provide general guidelines, physicians should also consider each patient’s individual risk factors, comorbidities, and preferences when deciding on the appropriate frequency of eye exams.

India’s Semaglutide Story Is Not Just About Diabetes. It’s About Pricing Disruption.

After India’s patent expiry, generic launches have entered the market at prices up to ~70% lower than Novo’s original products.

Novo’s Ozempic and Wegovy in India were roughly in the ₹8,800 to ₹11,000+ per month range. In comparison, Indian launches are now appearing anywhere from roughly ₹750 to ₹4,200, depending on the company, dose, format, and device positioning.

1⃣Now Look at Indian Launches

🔹Sun: ₹750 to ₹2,000 (per weekly dose depending on strength)
🔹Glenmark: ₹1,300 to ₹1,760 (per weekly dose)

2⃣This Changes the Debate Completely
Once a therapy moves from ₹10,000 a month to ₹1,500 to ₹3,000 a month, the market is no longer about brand substitution.

It becomes about demand unlocking.

And that is the big thing many people are missing.

3⃣Why the Typical Pharma Framework Fails Here

Most investors are still analysing semaglutide in India like a classic generic pharma event:

Patent expires → multiple entrants → prices fall → margins compress.

That framework is too simplistic.

Because semaglutide in India was not sitting in a fully penetrated market waiting for cheaper competition.

It was sitting in a market with massive disease burden but very low affordability-led penetration.

4⃣The Real Market Size Is Hidden in Affordability

India already has around 89.8 million adults living with diabetes, and this number is expected to rise to 156.7 million by 2050.

On the obesity side, the long-term burden is even larger, with around 254 million adults with generalised obesity and 351 million with abdominal obesity.

This is not just a substitution story from Novo to generics.

This is a market creation story driven by affordability.

5⃣Where Will Value Actually Accrue?

Not equally across the value chain.

API manufacturing may see the fastest commoditisation if too many players enter.

Plain formulations may benefit from volume growth, but differentiation will be limited.

Devices may hold better economics because patient comfort, convenience, dosing accuracy, and adherence matter significantly in chronic therapies.

Distribution and doctor trust may be the most underrated moat, because this is not a one-time prescription category. This is a long-term therapy where continuity matters.

6⃣Competition Will Be Brutal

Competition is going to intensify rapidly.

Reuters suggests that more than 40 Indian companies could launch over 50 brands in this space.

That is both the opportunity and the warning sign.

The opportunity is clear.

The Indian semaglutide market is now expected to grow from around ₹15 billion to nearly ₹80 billion by 2030.

That is not just expansion. That is category creation.

7⃣But Not Everyone Will Win

In markets like this, the first wave gets attention.

The second wave decides margins.

As more players enter and capacity builds, pricing pressure will accelerate, especially in low-differentiation formats like vials.

Not every company entering this space will create shareholder value.

8⃣The Underappreciated Angle: Exports

This is not just an India story.

Indian pharma companies are already looking at markets such as Canada, Brazil, Latin America, and Turkey.

This matters because India can become a low-cost manufacturing base for global price-sensitive markets.

So the real question is not just who wins India.

It is who uses India as a platform to scale globally.

9⃣Risks That Cannot Be Ignored

This is not a straight-line opportunity.

Pricing pressure can become too aggressive, especially in plain generic formats.

Regulatory scrutiny is already increasing. CDSCO has inspected multiple entities and acted against unauthorised sales, misleading promotions, and irregular distribution practices.

Compliance and channel discipline may become far more important than many investors currently expect.

There is also innovation risk. Globally, newer obesity therapies, next-generation GLP-1 drugs, and improved delivery systems are already being developed. This could reshape the competitive landscape again over the next few years.

📌Final Takeaway

On the surface, this may look like a generic price war.

But underneath, it is the emergence of a massive chronic metabolic category moving from premium to accessible.

Over the next three to five years, the biggest winners may not be the cheapest players.

They are more likely to be companies that combine scale, device quality, doctor trust, patient adherence economics, export optionality, and regulatory discipline.

The molecule may commoditise.

But the market may not.

And that is where the real value will be created.

This is the conversation the peptide and supplement space has been avoiding.

“Not for human use — for research purposes only” is the legal disclaimer that allows companies to sell compounds directly to consumers without FDA oversight, without purity verification requirements, without dosing standardization, and without any accountability for what’s actually in the vial or capsule.

Everyone in the space knows what’s happening. The company knows. The consumer knows. The influencer with the affiliate link knows. The “research purposes” label is a legal fiction that allows an unregulated supply chain to operate in plain sight.

Here’s what that means from the lab side.

When a pharmaceutical product goes through FDA approval, it’s subject to Current Good Manufacturing Practice requirements. Every batch is tested for identity, purity, potency, and contaminants. Every step of production is documented. The compound in the vial is verified to be what the label says it is, at the concentration the label claims, free of heavy metals, endotoxins, and microbial contamination.

When a gray market “research chemical” ships to your door, none of that applies. The label says BPC-157. Or semaglutide. Or whatever the compound of the month is. But nobody with regulatory authority verified the contents. The purity could be 98%. It could be 60%. It could contain degradation products, synthesis byproducts, or bacterial endotoxins that produce an inflammatory response the moment you inject them. You don’t know. The company doesn’t have to tell you. And the “not for human use” label is the legal shield that makes the entire arrangement possible.

The person injecting a gray market peptide based on a PubMed citation and an influencer’s discount code is trusting the most important decision in their health — what enters their bloodstream — to a supply chain with zero verification, zero accountability, and a legal disclaimer that explicitly says it wasn’t made for them.

Compounding pharmacies operate under state pharmacy board oversight with licensed pharmacists, verified ingredients, and standardized preparation protocols. They’re not perfect. But the difference between a compounding pharmacy and a gray market research chemical vendor is the difference between a lab with quality control and a website with a checkout button.

The crackdown is overdue. And the people most affected will be the ones who never asked the most basic question before injecting something into their body.

What’s actually in this. Who verified it. And where’s the certificate of analysis.

Don’t wait for the diagnosis.

Read the label.

Especially when the label says it wasn’t made for you.

GLP-1 receptors aren't only in your gut. The FDA's approval of Novo Nordisk's Wegovy HD (semaglutide 7.2 mg once-weekly injection) represents a meaningful advancement in obesity treatment. Granted under the agency's accelerated Commissioner's National Priority Voucher program in just 54 days, the new dose is indicated for adults with obesity (BMI ≥30) or overweight with comorbidities who have tolerated the standard 2.4 mg dose for at least four weeks and require additional clinically meaningful weight loss, always in combination with diet and exercise. This escalation builds on the established GLP-1 receptor agonist profile, offering a higher-efficacy option within the same proven molecule.

Data from the pivotal 72-week STEP UP trial (n=1,407 adults with obesity, no diabetes) showed participants on 7.2 mg achieving approximately 20.7% mean weight loss (full adherence scenario), compared with about 17.5% on 2.4 mg and 2-4% on placebo. In the more real-world treatment-regimen analysis, the higher dose delivered roughly 19% mean loss, with around one in three patients reaching the transformative 25%+ threshold - far more than on the lower dose or placebo. A companion study in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes confirmed 14.1% mean loss, and safety remained consistent with the class, primarily involving manageable gastrointestinal side effects that typically diminish over time.

In an increasingly competitive GLP-1 landscape, this dose optimization strengthens Novo's portfolio by helping more patients achieve profound, sustained outcomes without switching therapies. It complements Wegovy's existing indications - including cardiovascular risk reduction—and arrives alongside the rollout of oral semaglutide, broadening access to meaningful cardiometabolic improvements, enhanced mobility, quality of life, and potentially broader benefits being explored in neurodegeneration research.

Novo plans to launch Wegovy HD in the US in April via a convenient single-dose pen. This development underscores how incremental refinements to established therapies can drive real-world impact in metabolic disease.

The 54-day approval is impressive on process speed, but the more interesting question is what Novo gets out of this timing and what it means for the competitive landscape they've been actively reshaping.

Novo spent the last year resolving Wegovy manufacturing shortages, which did two things simultaneously. It removed semaglutide from FDA's drug shortage database, and that evaporated the legal justification for compounding pharmacies to mass-distribute cheaper alternatives. FDA issued a warning letter to Hims in February 2025 over exactly this, forcing them to discontinue compounded semaglutide while Novo filed a parallel patent infringement lawsuit. The shortage resolution wasn't just a supply chain win, it was a regulatory strategy that eliminated a billion-dollar gray market threatening their pricing power.

Now Wegovy HD at 7.2 mg extends the branded franchise upward right as the compounding competitors are being cleared off the field. Novo doesn't just get a new SKU, they get a higher-dose product launching into a market where the cheap alternatives that were creating pricing pressure no longer exist. If patients had reliable access to $250/month compounded semaglutide, policymakers would be asking hard questions about why brand products cost five times as much. That pressure is gone now.

The National Priority Voucher program accelerating this is real innovation in regulatory process. But the business context matters: Novo is simultaneously using FDA enforcement, patent litigation, and accelerated approvals as complementary tools to lock down the GLP-1 market. It included ~132,000 GLP-1RA users (semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, exenatide, dulaglutide) and ~201,000 sulfonylurea users as active comparators, followed up to 3 years.

**Key findings**:
- Continuous GLP-1RA use for 3 years conferred an **18% relative reduction** in major adverse cardiovascular events (**MACE**: myocardial infarction, stroke, or all-cause mortality) versus sulfonylureas, equating to ~4 fewer events per 100 people over 3 years.
- Benefit accumulated slowly: negligible before ~18 months, ~7% reduction by 2 years, ~15% by 2–2.5 years, reaching maximal at 3 years.
- Interruptions (≥6-month gaps) reduced net benefit to ~12% even with resumption.
- Discontinuation rapidly reversed protection: 6-month interruption linked to 4–8% increased MACE risk; 1 year off raised risk by 14%; 2 years off by 22%, essentially nullifying accumulated benefit.
- Risk elevation began within 6 months of stopping and approached or exceeded comparator levels within 1–1.5 years—roughly half the time needed to accrue full protection.
- In the cohort, 26% fully discontinued GLP-1RAs and 23% had ≥1 qualifying interruption.

This aligns with prior RCT evidence (e.g., SELECT trial: 20% MACE reduction with semaglutide 2.4 mg in non-diabetic overweight/obese adults with CVD; LEADER: 13% with liraglutide). Benefits arise partly independently of weight loss via direct GLP-1 receptor effects in cardiac/vascular tissue: reduced inflammation (e.g., CRP), improved endothelial function, plaque stabilization, modest BP lowering (~5 mmHg systolic), and triglyceride reduction.

Discontinuation triggers rapid "metabolic whiplash": weight regain (two-thirds of loss within 1 year per STEP 1 extension), HbA1c rebound (+0.25–0.65%), resurgence of BP, lipids, CRP, insulin resistance, and visceral fat—explaining swift loss of cardioprotection. Real-world discontinuation rates remain high (50–75% within 1 year) due to GI side effects, cost, insurance barriers, and supply constraints.

**Limitations**: Predominantly older male veterans with T2D and elevated baseline CV risk; results may not fully generalize to younger populations, non-diabetic obesity patients, or those maintaining weight via lifestyle. Observational design risks residual confounding despite target-trial emulation and active-comparator approach; no detailed weight trajectories or combination-therapy data.

**Implications**: GLP-1RAs function as chronic therapy for sustained CV risk reduction, similar to statins. Clinicians should prioritize adherence via gradual titration, insurance navigation, multidisciplinary support, and early identification of discontinuation risks. Payers denying ongoing coverage post-weight-loss goals may inadvertently increase MACE exposure. Future studies should explore maintenance dosing, intermittent regimens, weight-independent benefit persistence, and broader populations.

In short: GLP-1RA CV protection builds gradually over years of continuous use but erodes rapidly—often within months to 1–2 years—upon stopping, underscoring the need for long-term commitment to preserve heart benefits.

This small collection of neurons plays a critical role in motivating behavior. It drives the reward response when an action is beneficial for survival, such as eating calorie-dense food or reproduction.

You eat. Satiety hormones such as GLP-1, CCK, PYY, and insulin rise. These signals reach the brain and tell you to stop.

GLP-1 receptors are widely distributed in the brain, including within the ventral tegmentum.

As GLP-1 signaling increases, dopamine output from the VTA decreases.

Let’s continue the series: “Dopamine and the Brain.”

As discussed in my previous post, several major dopamine-producing neurons exist in the brain. Many originate in the midbrain, also known scientifically as the mesencephalon.

As mentioned previously, one of the most important dopamine-producing regions is the substantia nigra (Latin for black substance).

This region produces dopamine so actively that neuromelanin accumulates as a metabolic byproduct, giving the tissue its characteristic dark appearance.

You need this region to move normally.

When the substantia nigra degenerates, dopamine production falls and patients develop Parkinson’s disease.

In the image I attached (pic 1), you are looking at a real midbrain specimen.

The black arrows point to the heavily pigmented substantia nigra.

Also appreciate the surrounding anatomy:

Blue arrow → Cerebral aqueduct

Around it lies the periaqueductal gray, an important pain-modulating region.

Can you spot cranial nerve III?

The red arrows likely highlight the internal cerebral veins, based on their posterior position and relationship to the thalamus.

Now let’s discuss another dopamine-producing region in the mesencephalon.

This region projects its axons to the limbic system.

This group of neurons is called the ventral tegmental area (VTA).

I circled it in red.

Like the substantia nigra, it also appears somewhat dark due to neuromelanin produced during dopamine metabolism, although it is typically less pigmented.

The VTA sends dopaminergic projections to the limbic system, which plays a central role in:

• emotion
• motivation
• reward
• behavior
• memory
This pathway is known as the mesolimbic dopamine pathway.
It is essentially the brain’s reward and reinforcement system.
This circuit links pleasure with memory, allowing you to remember which experiences were rewarding and motivating you to seek them again.
This system helps rank pleasurable experiences.

That cupcake.

That drug.

That experience.

The limbic system reinforces the behavior and motivates you to seek it again.

This is one of the fundamental circuits underlying addiction, including food addiction.

So here is a question:

What nucleus in the basal ganglia receives dopamine projections from the VTA?

This nucleus contains dopamine receptors that respond to VTA output, similar to how the striatum receives dopamine from the substantia nigra to regulate movement (see my previous post for details).

Now consider this clinical scenario.

A 75-year-old patient with Parkinson’s disease is started on pramipexole, a dopamine agonist (a drug that stimulates dopamine receptors).

The goal is to stimulate dopamine receptors in the striatum, because the degenerating substantia nigra is no longer producing sufficient dopamine.

But dopamine receptors are not limited to the motor system.

They are also present in the mesolimbic reward circuit, particularly in the nucleus accumbens.

So what happens?

The medication stimulates those receptors as well.

The patient suddenly develops compulsive gambling, hypersexuality, or food addiction.

In other words, the medication itself can create addictive behavior.

This illustrates an important point:

Human behavior is clearly not driven by “willpower” alone.

Dopamine and the brain.

The first image shows dopaminergic circuits throughout the brain. As you can see, dopamine projections are widespread.

The blue pathways represent dopaminergic projections, which primarily originate from midbrain structures such as the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and the substantia nigra.

Although the neurotransmitter dopamine often gets a bad reputation because of its role in addiction (including food addiction), it is one of the most important neurotransmitters in the brain.

Cocaine, for example, produces its powerful effects by blocking the dopamine transporter (DAT). This blockade ultimately leads to an increase in dopamine levels in reward circuits of the brain, particularly in the nucleus accumbens (NAc in pic 2), producing the intense feeling of euphoria.

Interestingly, GLP-1 agonists appear to modulate these reward circuits. Evidence suggests GLP-1 signaling can influence dopaminergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) of the midbrain, altering dopamine signaling involved in reward (such as the nucleus accumbens, NAc in pic 2) and food intake.

But what is the relationship between dopaminergic neurons, dopamine, and movement?

You need dopamine to help you move in a fast and efficient manner.

Too much dopamine acutely in certain brain circuits, such as during acute cocaine intoxication, can produce restlessness, fidgeting, pacing, and what is sometimes referred to as “crack dancing.”

Not enough dopamine in certain circuits - particularly the nigrostriatal pathway (see pic 3, green projection) - means you become slow. 

If this loss of dopamine is progressive, it leads to diseases of impaired movement such as Parkinson’s disease.

The course of Hidradenitis Suppurativa (HS)

 is chronic and unpredictable, following a relapsing-remitting pattern of painful flares interspersed with periods of lower activity or remission. 

It usually starts after puberty (late teens to early 30s, average onset around age 22) and can last decades 

— one study found an average disease duration of nearly 19 years at the time of survey, with most people still experiencing active disease. Flares involve tender, boil-like nodules or abscesses that last about 7 days on average (patients report roughly 2 new lesions per month), 

often with pus drainage, odour, and slow healing. 

Aggravating factors include heat/sweating, friction, stress, fatigue, tight clothing, and (in many women) menstruation. In women, symptoms sometimes ease after menopause. 
pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.go

Management of HS

 has no cure but is highly effective at controlling flares, 

reducing pain/scarring, preventing progression, and improving daily life.

1. Lifestyle & Supportive Care (foundation for ALL stages)Quit smoking (biggest modifiable factor — dramatically improves remission rates).  

Weight loss if overweight (even modest loss helps; some newer data on GLP-1 medications like semaglutide).  

Gentle skin care: antiseptic washes (e.g., chlorhexidine or benzoyl peroxide), avoid shaving/trauma/irritants, wear loose clothing, 

use warm compresses for flares. 
 
Wound care for draining lesions; pain management (NSAIDs, paracetamol, or specialist input).  
Mental health support 

— HS can be isolating and distressing.

2. Medical Treatments (anti-inflammatory focus)Mild (Stage I) or occasional flares: Topical clindamycin, resorcinol cream, or intralesional steroid injections into nodules.  

Moderate (Stage II) or frequent flares: Oral antibiotics (doxycycline or minocycline for months; 

or clindamycin + rifampicin combination for 8–12 weeks)

 — these work mainly as anti-inflammatories, not just against bacteria. 

Hormonal options for women (combined oral contraceptives or 
Bimekizumab (dual IL-17A/F inhibitor) 

— approved for adults in recent years.
Other options (off-label or emerging): 

infliximab, ustekinumab, retinoids, or metformin.

Acute secondary bacterial infections (common in open lesions): Short-course targeted antibiotics + drainage if needed, but the real prevention is controlling the underlying HS inflammation.

3. Procedural & Surgical OptionsAcute abscesses:

 Simple incision & drainage for immediate relief (but not long-term solution).  

Chronic tunnels/scarring: “Deroofing/unroofing” (removes the roof of sinus tracts

 — highly effective with lower recurrence), wide local excision, or laser therapy.

 Surgery works best when combined with biologics (reduces recurrence).  
Other: Intense pulsed light or Nd:YAG laser for milder cases.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has issued a formal warning letter dated March 5, 2026, to Novo Nordisk, the manufacturer of widely prescribed GLP-1 medications including Ozempic (semaglutide), Wegovy (semaglutide), and Saxenda (liraglutide).

• Not following up on a patient death associated with semaglutide, citing lack of consent from the reporter—despite regulations not requiring such consent for PADE investigations.

These lapses raise important questions about the integrity of post-marketing safety surveillance for GLP-1 receptor agonists, a class of drugs now used by an estimated 1 in 8 U.S. adults (over 31 million people), according to recent polling data.

Bimagrumab doesn't bring us closer to immortality. At least, that's what biochemist Charles Brenner says — and he's challenging the whole "we're almost at LEV" narrative.

On March 2, 2026, immunologist Derya Unutmaz tweeted: "This one drug, Bimagrumab, is likely to add another year to average lifespan, probably more! We are getting close to longevity escape velocity."

Hours later, Brenner responded. He's the City of Hope biochemist who discovered nicotinamide riboside metabolism pathways to NAD+:

"The drug preserving muscle mass is very impressive. But you would have to believe that lean people — or any lean mammal — encode the capacity for immortality to believe this means we're closer to LEV. Mammals encode developmental timing that governs our lifespans. Bimagrumab doesn't change that."

Here's what bimagrumab actually does: it's a monoclonal antibody blocking the ACVR2B receptor. Block that receptor, and muscle tissue doesn't break down even during weight loss. Novartis developed it for inclusion body myositis, failed phase IIb/III. Eli Lilly bought Versanis Bio for $1.9 billion in July 2023 and pivoted to obesity. In March 2026, Nature Medicine published phase IIb results: bimagrumab + semaglutide beats semaglutide alone for fat mass reduction.

Zero data on lifespan extension — not in mice, not in humans. Unutmaz's claim is extrapolation from metabolic markers.

Longevity Escape Velocity itself? Term coined by Aubrey de Grey (PLoS Biology, 2004): the point where each year lived adds more than a year to expected lifespan. Kurzweil in 2018 said 2028–2030, moved it to 2029–2035 in 2024. de Grey gives 50% probability for mid-to-late 2030s. George Church: "Wouldn't be surprised if 2050." Peter Ottsjö introduced Science Escape Velocity — the critical mass of knowledge needed to create therapies.

Brenner's thesis: bimagrumab preserves muscle but doesn't touch the aging program. Mammals have a species-specific developmental program that sets lifespan. Statins, semaglutide, bimagrumab — these are symptomatic interventions. They delay specific causes of death. Epigenetic reprogramming, senolytics, telomerase activation — those are programmatic interventions targeting the aging program itself. LEV, by Brenner's logic, requires the second type. The first adds years but doesn't change the curve.

Brenner isn't a gerontologist. He's a biochemist studying NAD metabolism and nicotinamide riboside — a field where a systematic review of 113 studies showed: NAD+ levels reliably rise in humans, but translation to measurable health improvements is heterogeneous. His developmental program thesis is a hypothesis, not consensus. de Grey, Sinclair, Church assume aging can be slowed by interventions. Brenner questions that premise.

His position echoes Tony Wyss-Coray: "There is no intervention tested and confirmed to extend human lifespan."

The absence of lifespan extension data is an infrastructure problem: calendar time for clinical trials hits the wall of endpoint duration and regulatory procedures. Compressing timelines needs surrogate endpoints that reliably predict late outcomes — and validating those surrogates takes years itself.

Until those tools exist, the LEV conversation remains a debate about predictions, not data.

Sulfur gas (hydrogen sulfide) in supplements often causes "sulfur burps" or foul-smelling gas due to the breakdown of compounds like MSM, chondroitin sulfate, or high-protein powders (whey/casein) by gut bacteria. These side effects are common with supplements containing sulfur, sulfites, or specific amino acids like cysteine. [1, 2, 3]  
Key Supplements and Causes 

• Common Sulfur-Containing Supplements: Methylsulfonylmethane (MSM), chondroitin sulfate, glucosamine sulfate, glutathione, and alpha-lipoic acid. 
• Protein Powders: Whey and casein often contain high levels of sulfur-containing amino acids (cysteine and methionine), which produce a rotten egg smell during digestion. 
• Other Potential Triggers: Iron supplements, multivitamins, and some medications (e.g., antibiotics, antacids). 
• GLP-1 Medications: Weight loss drugs like Ozempic, Wegovy, or Zepbound can cause delayed stomach emptying, leading to a buildup of hydrogen sulfide gas. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]  

Management and Tips 

• Reduce Dosage: Lower the amount of the supplement causing issues. 
• Improve Digestion: Eat smaller meals, chew food slowly, and stay hydrated. 
• Over-the-Counter Solutions: Pepto-Bismol (bismuth subsalicylate) can help by binding to the sulfur in the gut. Verywell Health 4587735 suggest using products like Gas-X (simethicone). 
• Dietary Adjustments: Reduce intake of sulfur-rich foods like eggs, dairy, garlic, and onions if you are taking these supplements. [6, 7, 9, 10, 11]

Weight-loss and diabetes drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy have completely transformed modern medicine. These treatments generated roughly $30 billion for the Danish manufacturer Novo Nordisk in 2025 alone. However, a major market shift is on the horizon.

The active ingredient in these "wonder drugs," known as semaglutide, is losing its patent protection in major markets like India, Brazil, and China later this month. This expiration, set for March 20 in India, is sparking a massive generic drug gold rush.

Currently, a month's supply of branded semaglutide sells for around $200 in the United States. In India, innovator prices range from ₹8,800 to over ₹16,000 per month. This high price point excludes roughly 25 percent of the population who desperately need these metabolic therapies.

But a recent study  using pricing information from other off-patent medicines, researchers calculated that semaglutide could cost as little as $3 a month to manufacture.

Dr. Samuel Cross of Imperial College London notes that bringing prices down to these sustainable levels could allow millions more people to access life-changing treatment for chronic conditions.

In India, highly anticipated generic versions are expected to retail between ₹3,000 and ₹5,000, dropping the price to less than half the cost of the innovator molecule.

Leading Indian pharmaceutical companies are primed for day-one launches. Drugmakers like Sun Pharma, Zydus Lifesciences, Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories, and Alkem Laboratories have already secured regulatory approvals.

Sun Pharma will introduce its weight-management injection as "Noveltreat," while Zydus plans to launch under brands like "SEMAGLYN" using a reusable, adjustable injection pen.

To defend its market share ahead of the patent cliff, Novo Nordisk has slashed its own prices. The company has also partnered with firms like Abbott and Emcure to expand its reach deeper into tier-1 and tier-2 Indian cities.

The medical benefits of this broader access are immense. Globally, clinical obesity causes 3.7 million deaths annually, while hundreds of millions suffer from Type 2 diabetes.

Semaglutide effectively mimics a naturally occurring gut hormone that signals fullness to the brain, leading to a typical weight loss of 10 to 15 kg alongside major anti-diabetic benefits. 

For India, home to an estimated 135 million diabetics, these cheaper alternatives represent a massive public health opportunity.

Yet, the explosion of cheap generics also brings significant medical concerns. Experts warn that as general practitioners and consulting physicians begin prescribing these drugs instead of specialists, strict patient profiling will be required.

Without specialized monitoring, there is a high risk of therapy dropouts. This is particularly concerning because patients who stop taking the drug typically regain weight and lose glycemic control much faster than those using lifestyle-based weight-loss programs.

Safety also remains a critical issue. While generally well-tolerated, common side effects include nausea and diarrhea, with rare but serious risks like gastroparesis, intestinal paralysis, and blindness. Lawsuits are currently mounting in the US over these severe adverse effects.

Public interest litigations in India emphasize the urgent need for a robust pharmacovigilance system to monitor safety and off-label misuse as millions more access the drug.

Ultimately, the semaglutide patent expiry could become a historic medical success story, akin to the mass production of affordable HIV and TB drugs. If monitored carefully, this breakthrough could revolutionize global health.

Animal studies provide the clearest evidence so far. 

In 2025 research published in preprint and peer-reviewed formats, long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonists like semaglutide markedly suppressed voluntary wheel running in both lean and diet-induced obese mice. 
This drop in spontaneous exercise was not simply due to reduced food intake but reflected a genuine decrease in motivation: treated animals showed far less willingness to exert effort in progressive ratio tasks, where increasing work (lever presses) was required to gain access to the running wheel. 

Researchers linked this behavioral shift to the drug's influence on central reward pathways, particularly dopamine signaling in brain regions like the nucleus accumbens, which GLP-1 agonists appear to blunt not only for food but for other rewarding activities including movement. Human data remain more indirect but increasingly suggestive. 

Clinicians and patients frequently report that after starting these therapies, the internal drive to exercise fades—many describe working out purely out of obligation rather than enjoyment or energy. While some real-world cohorts show small increases in structured activity as weight loss eases joint strain and breathing, the spontaneous, pleasure-driven movement that sustains long-term fitness often declines.

Losing muscle mass compounds the issue: lower strength and VO₂ max heighten risks for frailty, falls, and eventual heart strain, especially in older or previously sedentary individuals. Is semaglutide now a heart medicine? What the 17,000‑person SELECT trial really showed.

In high‑risk people with heart disease and extra weight but no diabetes, this “skinny jab” also clearly lowered heart attacks and strokes over several years.

Weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg cut major cardiovascular events by 20% in people with obesity, established CVD, and no diabetes. The SELECT trial was a multicentre, double‑blind RCT enrolling 17,604 adults ≥45 years with BMI ≥27 and established atherosclerotic CVD but no history of diabetes, randomised to once‑weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg or placebo plus standard care. Over a mean 39.8 months’ follow‑up, the primary composite (CV death, non‑fatal MI, non‑fatal stroke) occurred in 6.5% of the semaglutide group vs 8.0% of placebo (HR 0.80; 95% CI 0.72–0.90). Prespecified analyses show this benefit is consistent across baseline HbA1c categories (normoglycaemia vs pre‑diabetes) and across adiposity strata, suggesting mechanisms beyond glycaemic control alone. Semaglutide produced sustained ~10–11% mean weight loss at 4 years vs ~1–2% with placebo, but with higher discontinuation mainly due to GI side‑effects (discontinuation ~16–27% vs ~8–24%, depending on analysis).
Wilding JPH et al., “Semaglutide and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Obesity without Diabetes,” New England Journal of Medicine, PMID: 37952131
Deanfield J et al., “Semaglutide and cardiovascular outcomes by baseline glycemia (SELECT analysis),” Diabetes Care 2024 (PMCID: PMC11282385).
My Take:

SELECT is a large, event‑driven RCT with hard outcomes and robust analyses, this is very high‑quality evidence. However, the enrolled population is specific: established CVD plus overweight/obesity; we do not have equivalent outcomes data for primary prevention in lower‑risk individuals or lean patients. Long‑term (>5–10 year) safety, cost‑effectiveness, and the impact of widespread use (including in lower‑risk groups) remain open questions.
For clinicians; continue to emphasise lifestyle foundations: diet quality, physical activity, sleep, BP and lipid control must remain first‑line; in SELECT, semaglutide was layered on top of standard care, not a substitute for it.

### Common Side Effects
Most are gastrointestinal and sometimes improve over time or with dose adjustments:
- Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, abdominal pain, and bloating.
- These affect a large portion of users initially but tend to lessen after weeks or months.

### Potential Long-Term or Serious Side Effects
Longer-term use (months to years) has been associated with several risks, based on clinical trials, post-marketing reports, and studies up to 2025–2026:
- **Gastrointestinal issues**: Gastroparesis (stomach paralysis), ileus (intestinal blockage), severe vomiting, or chronic GI problems. These can lead to malnutrition, dehydration, or hospitalization in rare cases.
- **Pancreatitis** (inflammation of the pancreas): Reported in some users; can be acute and severe, potentially leading to long-term pancreatic damage.
- **Gallbladder problems**: Including gallstones or cholecystitis, often linked to rapid weight loss.
- **Kidney injury**: Acute kidney issues or worsening of chronic kidney disease, sometimes requiring monitoring.
- **Vision changes**: Including diabetic retinopathy complications or rare associations with conditions like non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION).
- **Skin changes**: "Ozempic face" — sagging, wrinkling, or hollowed appearance due to rapid facial fat loss (not unique to these drugs but common with any fast weight reduction).
- **Thyroid tumors/cancer**: A boxed warning (FDA's strongest) exists for possible thyroid C-cell tumors, including medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), based on rodent studies. Human data is mixed — some studies show no significant increased risk in most users, while others suggest a potential slight elevation (especially after 1–3 years). It's contraindicated in those with personal/family history of MTC or MEN2 syndrome.
- **Other**: Muscle loss (sarcopenia) from rapid weight reduction, potential nutrient deficiencies, gallbladder disease, and rare reports of mental health concerns (though large reviews have not confirmed causation for issues like suicidal ideation).

Many serious side effects are rare, and long-term data (from trials up to 4+ years) show benefits often outweigh risks for appropriate patients, with cardiovascular protections noted in some approvals.

### Is Death a Concern?
Death is **extremely rare** and not a common or established direct outcome from proper use of these drugs. No large-scale evidence shows these medications commonly cause fatal events in typical patients.

However:
- Rare deaths have been reported in adverse event databases (e.g., UK MHRA data up to 2025 linked dozens of deaths to GLP-1 drugs, some tied to diabetes treatment, others to weight loss use; similar U.S. FAERS reports exist).
- These are often associated with severe complications (e.g., pancreatitis leading to complications, bowel obstructions, or misuse/overdose), pre-existing conditions, or counterfeit/compounded versions.
- Overdose or improper use can increase risks of severe hypoglycemia, seizures, or other life-threatening issues.
- Overall, population studies and reviews emphasize that while serious adverse events occur, the drugs' mortality risk appears low compared to obesity-related risks (e.g., heart disease, stroke), and some data show reduced cardiovascular death in high-risk groups.

These medications require medical supervision, especially long-term. Risks vary by individual factors (e.g., dose, duration, health history). Always consult a healthcare provider for personalized advice, as they can monitor for issues and weigh benefits vs. risks. Data continues to evolve with ongoing studies.

Novo Nordisk’s $NVO CagriSema "Miss" Is A Reality Check, But Is The Market Overreacting Again 

The market is having another one of its tantrums. Novo Nordisk $NVO took a massive 15% hit after the headline read that its next-generation obesity shot, CagriSema, "fell short" of Eli Lilly’s $LLY tirzepatide. 

If you’ve been following my previous analysis, you know I’ve called Novo one of the most asymmetric value opportunities in healthcare, but even I have to admit: this trial result is a punch to the gut. 

In a head-to-head trial, patients on a standard dose of CagriSema achieved 20.2% weight loss over 84 weeks. 

Meanwhile, Lilly’s tirzepatide (Zepbound) clocked in at 23.6%. That 3.4% gap might not seem like much to a layperson, but in this high-stakes game it's the difference between being the gold standard and being an expensive runner-up. 

The market responded by wiping billions off Novo’s valuation, which has now cratered more than 60% over the past year. 

Is the Comparison Fair?

Before we declare Eli Lilly the king of the hill, let’s look at the practical interpretation of this data. This specific trial used a "standard dose" of CagriSema. 

Novo has been quick to point out that another trial is reading out later this year where patients will be pushed to the highest dose. 

There is a legitimate argument that Novo’s trial designs have been too conservative, effectively holding back the drug’s potential to avoid side effects.

If the high dose trial shows results north of 25%, the narrative changes overnight. But right now, Novo is in a "show me" state. 

CagriSema was supposed to be the "Lilly Killer" a combination of semaglutide (the stuff in Ozempic) and an amylin mimic. 

The fact that it couldn't beat tirzepatide on a standard-dose basis suggests that Lilly’s dual-agonist approach (GLP-1 and GIP) might just be a more efficient biological lever.
